analysis.one_liner: Bans union recognition without a government-run secret ballot election, blocking card-check organizing.
analysis.headline: Backed by 72 House Republicans, the bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Democratic-controlled House and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it illegal for an employer to recognize a union unless the union first won a secret ballot election run by the National Labor Relations Board. It would also make it illegal for a union to pressure an employer into such recognition. Today, employers and unions are allowed to skip the election and use signed cards from a majority of workers instead; the bill would shut that route down.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who want to keep unions out gain the most. The bill would make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to sign a voluntary recognition or neutrality agreement, which shields businesses from union campaigns built on signed authorization cards and gives companies that resist organizing a federal rule on their side.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new unfair labor practice: an employer may not recognize or bargain with a union unless the union was chosen by a majority of employees in a secret ballot election run by the National Labor Relations Board.

It also makes it an unfair labor practice for a union to cause or attempt to cause an employer to recognize a union that did not win such an election, cutting off organizing campaigns built on signed authorization cards.
Existing bargaining relationships recognized before the bill's enactment would be grandfathered in, so current union contracts would not be undone.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who want to form a union would lose the fastest route to recognition. Under current law, an employer can voluntarily recognize a union once a majority of employees sign cards; this bill would force every new organizing drive through an NLRB election, a process that takes months and that employers can contest, while union campaigns would be barred from pressuring companies to recognize them.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argue that a secret ballot run by the government is the only method that ensures a choice free of coercion or intimidation, and the bill's findings state that recognition by private agreement threatens employees' freedom to choose.

The bill would eliminate voluntary recognition, the fastest route to a union contract, and force workers into an election process that employers can drag out through objections and litigation, during which workers who support the union have no contract protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated benefit — protecting workers from pressure when deciding on union representation — comes at the cost of removing the one legal path that lets workers organize without a drawn-out election campaign. Because it would make voluntary recognition itself illegal, its practical effect falls on workers and unions seeking representation, while employers that oppose unions gain a new federal shield. The costs to organizing workers are larger than the protection it offers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee, got referred to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2007, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On May 18, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
Democrats held the House majority during this Congress, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions that rely on card-check recognition are better off, because the existing system remains intact. Employers that wanted a federal ban on voluntary recognition lost their window, as the bill was never scheduled in the Democratic-controlled House.

for.name: Rep. Charles Norwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the original Republican cosponsor list.

for.name: 72 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: Rep. George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in his committee; it was referred to a subcommittee and stayed there.

against.name: Organized labor
against.what_they_did: Opposed secret-ballot-mandate bills like this one because they would ban card-check recognition, and backed the rival Employee Free Choice Act instead.

sides.party_line_note: All 72 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat touched the bill; it died in committee under a Democratic chairman.

industries.note: The bill would make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to recognize a union without an NLRB election, giving businesses a legal shield against union card-check campaigns and neutrality agreements. Workers who want a union would have to win a contested election the employer can delay.

Unions would be barred from organizing through signed authorization cards and from pressuring employers to recognize them, eliminating the fastest and least adversarial route to representation. Union membership growth depends heavily on that route.
